To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the incidence of plasmids in K1 strains is high, that plasmids of similar sizes occur in strains of the same O serogroup, that there is an association between plasmid type and serotype, and that plasmid type is not related to the site of isolation of the K1 strains or their ability to cause meningitis.

the K1 strains of E. coli from neonates with meningitides and from healthy individuals have similar plasmid profiles, hemolysin patterns, and colicin profiles, and that the plasmids of the O18 strains of E. col are similar.
all 62 E. coli K1 strains possessed plasmid DNA and that 51 of 62 strains had multiple plasmids.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epidemiology of E. coli strains that cause neonatal meningitis, with particular reference to the K1 capsule.
the epidemiology of the K1 capsulated strain of Escherichria coli, a common cause of neonatal meningitis.
the epidemiology of Escherichica coli K1, a capsular serotype that is a major cause of bacterial meningitis in neonates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the K1 strains of E. coli isolated from neonates with meningitits are not more virulent than those isolated from the feces of healthy individuals.

there are no differences in the plasmid content, hemolysin production, colicin production, or hemagglutinin production between E. coli K1 strains isolated during meningitis or from healthy individuals.

the K1 capsulated strains of E. coli isolated from neonates with meningitides and those isolated from healthy individuals of all age groups have similar plasmids and similar metabolic characteristics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the plasmid content of E. coli strains is not a useful indicator of virulence or the source of the organism.
the plasmid profiles of K1 strains isolated during neonatal meningitis are similar to the plasmid content of K1 strains from healthy individuals.
the plasmid profile of E. coli K1 is similar in all clinical and nonclinical isolates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are no differences in the virulence genes of E. coli K1 strains isolated in the cerebrospinals fluids of neonates or in the stools of healthy adults.
we have developed a method for isolating the plasmid DNA from the bacterial cell.
we can now use the plasmid content to identify the strain of E. coli K1.
